turns.prompt_text: I'm learning about the uniformity of throwing a die I know the graph for throwing a die is uniform over the six choices given infinite throws, that is, there's uniform one in six chance of each face However, if you throw a pair of die, then you have the output 1 through 12, and if the function used to determine the output is addition, then there are equal chances of rolling 2 or 12, 3 or 11, 4 or 10, 5 or 9, 6 or 8, or 7, where seven has the most likelihood of being thrown?
turns.response_html:
You have hit the nail right on the head! Your intuition is completely correct.

When you roll a single die, the probability distribution is uniform—every outcome ($1$ through $6$) has an equal probability of $\frac{1}{6}$.

However, when you roll a pair of dice and add the results together, the distribution changes from flat and uniform to symmetric and triangular.

Here is exactly why that happens and how the math breaks down.

The Sample Space ($6 \times 6 = 36$)

While a single die has $6$ possible outcomes, a pair of dice has $36$ possible combinations ($6 \text{ faces} \times 6 \text{ faces}$). Even though the total score ranges from $2$ to $12$ (not $1$ to $12$, since the lowest possible roll is $1 + 1 = 2$), the combinations are not distributed evenly across those sums.

There is only one way to roll a total of $2$ or $12$, but there are six different ways to roll a total of $7$.

Breakdown of Combinations

Because each individual die outcome is independent and uniform, we can count the number of ways to achieve each sum to find its exact probability out of $36$:

SumPossible Combinations (Die 1, Die 2)Number of WaysProbability
2$(1,1)$1$\frac{1}{36}$
3$(1,2), (2,1)$2$\frac{2}{36}$
4$(1,3), (2,2), (3,1)$3$\frac{3}{36}$
5$(1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1)$4$\frac{4}{36}$
6$(1,5), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1)$5$\frac{5}{36}$
7$(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$6$\frac{6}{36}$ ($\frac{1}{6}$)
8$(2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2)$5$\frac{5}{36}$
9$(3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3)$4$\frac{4}{36}$
10$(4,6), (5,5), (6,4)$3$\frac{3}{36}$
11$(5,6), (6,5)$2$\frac{2}{36}$
12$(6,6)$1$\frac{1}{36}$

Why 7 is the Peak

As you perfectly noted, the probabilities mirror each other perfectly as you move away from the center ($2$ pairs with $12$, $3$ with $11$, and so on).

The number $7$ sits at the absolute peak of this distribution because it has the highest number of degrees of freedom. Every single number on the first die has a corresponding "partner" number on the second die that can successfully add up to $7$. For example, if you roll a $1$, you need a $6$; if you roll a $4$, you need a $3$.

For extreme sums like $2$ or $12$, you have no flexibility—you are entirely dependent on rolling perfect pairs ($(1,1)$ or $(6,6)$).

This transition from a flat uniform distribution to a peaked distribution is actually a foundational concept in statistics. If you were to keep adding more dice (3, 4, 5, or more) and adding their totals together, that distribution curve would start looking less like a sharp triangle and more like a smooth, bell-shaped Normal Distribution (thanks to the Central Limit Theorem).

turns.prompt_text: Let's stick to 2 die for now, what would be the probability of rolling any one of the outcomes? 2. Through 12
turns.response_html:
When we look at the probability of rolling any single one of those outcomes individually, we use the values from the distribution table we just looked at.

Since there are $36$ total possible ways the two dice can land, you just divide the number of successful combinations for that specific sum by $36$.

Here is the exact probability for each individual outcome, written as fractions, decimals, and percentages:

SumNumber of CombinationsProbability (Fraction)Probability (Decimal)Probability (Percentage)
2 or 121 way$\frac{1}{36}$~0.0282.8%
3 or 112 ways$\frac{2}{36}$ (or $\frac{1}{18}$)~0.0565.6%
4 or 103 ways$\frac{3}{36}$ (or $\frac{1}{12}$)~0.0838.3%
5 or 94 ways$\frac{4}{36}$ (or $\frac{1}{9}$)~0.11111.1%
6 or 85 ways$\frac{5}{36}$~0.13913.9%
76 ways$\frac{6}{36}$ (or $\frac{1}{6}$)~0.16716.7%

A Cool Pattern to Notice

Because the distribution is perfectly symmetrical, there is a really easy trick to remember the odds:

  • For any sum from 2 to 7, the number of ways to roll it is just $(\text{Sum} - 1)$. (e.g., There are $4$ ways to roll a $5$).
  • For any sum from 7 to 12, the number of ways to roll it is $(13 - \text{Sum})$. (e.g., There are $3$ ways to roll a $10$).

If you add up all $36$ individual combinations ($\frac{1}{36} + \frac{2}{36} + \dots + \frac{1}{36}$), you get exactly $\frac{36}{36}$, which equals $1$, or a 100% chance that one of these outcomes will happen on any given throw.

turns.prompt_text: That helps quite a bit. Another question I have is if I had a bunch of dice and I just kept rolling them in pairs, how long would it take for me to actually discover this uniform? I guess I'm asking how long does the error take to even out?
turns.response_html:
What you are asking about is one of the most famous and practical concepts in statistics: the Law of Large Numbers and the concept of statistical convergence.

The short answer is that you will start to see the general "triangle" shape surprisingly quickly (around 30 to 50 rolls), but to get the error to truly "even out" so that your real-world percentages precisely match the theoretical math, you need hundreds or thousands of rolls.

Statistsics views this "error evening out" across three distinct phases:

Phase 1: The "Chaos" Phase (1 to 20 rolls)

At this stage, randomness rules. Because you have so few data points, a single lucky streak can completely distort your graph.

  • What you'll see: You might roll three $12$s in a row just by pure chance. Your graph won't look like a triangle at all; it might look completely flat, or skewed, or have a massive spike at $4$.
  • The Error: Extremely high.

Phase 2: The "Blurry Triangle" Phase (30 to 100 rolls)

This is the inflection point where the underlying math finally starts to overpower the raw randomness.

  • What you'll see: By $50$ rolls, the center numbers ($6, 7, 8$) will almost certainly have taller bars on your graph than the extreme numbers ($2, 12$). The triangle shape is clearly visible, but it will look "noisy" or jagged. 7 might be winning, but maybe 6 accidentally has a few more counts than it should.
  • The Error: Noticeable, but the pattern is undeniable.

Phase 3: The "True Uniform" Phase (500+ rolls)

To get the actual experimental percentages to tightly align with the theoretical percentages (like hitting exactly $16.7%$ for rolling a $7$), you have to keep going.

Here is a general rule of thumb for how the error shrinks as you keep rolling:

  • At 100 rolls: Your results will generally be within $\pm 5%$ of the true probability. (Your $7$s might show up $21%$ of the time instead of $16.7%$).
  • At 1,000 rolls: Your margin of error drops to roughly $\pm 1.5%$. The distribution curve looks beautifully smooth and symmetrical.
  • At 10,000 rolls: The error shrinks to less than $\pm 0.5%$.

Why does it take so long?

The trick is that the absolute number of weird anomalies actually goes up, but their relative percentage shrinks.

If you roll a pair of dice $10$ times, and get an extra two $12$s by pure luck, that mistake accounts for $20%$ of your total data—completely ruining your graph. If you roll the dice $1,000$ times, and get an extra two $12$s, that mistake only accounts for $0.2%$ of your data, making it an invisible blip on an otherwise perfect triangle.
